segments.text: AcmeCX's
risk model flags the riskiest 10% of
refunds. In this synthetic data, fraud
is 3 and 1/2% in every language.
Legitimate English-speaking customers
are flagged 3.9% of the time. Hindi
speakers, 13.2. Hinglish speakers, 16.9.
More than four times as often. And the
intervals don't overlap. This isn't
noise.
Lesson 36. A lab, we find a fairness
gap, fix it, and write down why.
The lab's data is built so we know the
truth. Behavior, like prior refunds and
account age, drives fraud. So true fraud
is the same in every language. But a
description quality score comes from an
English-centric model. It's lower for
Hindi and Hinglish, and only slightly
lower for fraud. A data scientist added
it to the risk model because it improves
overall detection. And the top 10% of
scores get flagged, which means delay
and suspicion.
Now look at the same model by region.
Metro, 9.2%.
Rural, 9.1. Tier 2, 9.1. Perfectly
balanced. Language is spread evenly
across regions, so the effect averages
away. Pick evaluation dimensions from
your harm analysis, not convenience.
Model A catches more fraud overall, 33
and 1/2%, but where? Only about a fifth
of English-speaking fraud. Over 40% of
Hindi fraud. And more than half of
Hinglish fraud. It concentrates flags on
non-English speakers. English fraud
slips through, and innocent Hindi and
Hinglish customers carry the burden.
Model B is the same model without the
description quality score. English,
Hindi, 8.5. Hinglish, 9.5. The intervals
overlap. The language ratio rises from
0.23 to 0.88. The price is about 19%
fewer frauds caught at the same review
capacity.
A business trade-off to decide and
document, not hide.
There's a third option from the notes
exercises. We computed it with the labs
own model. Model A fails with a ratio of
0.23. Model A with a separate threshold
per language equalizes false positives
and catches the most fraud of all.
Model B catches less and passes. So, why
reject thresholds? They use language
explicitly in each decision, which needs
legal review. And they leave the biased
feature in place, treating the symptom.
A multilingual quality score is tracked
as the real fix.
Model B's intersection table shows
ratios as low as 0.7. Should we panic?
English metro, about 9.8%
with a narrow interval. Hinglish tier
two, 10.3. Hindi rural, 7.3 from just
445 requests. Its interval spans 5 to
10%. The smallest of nine noisy
estimates is biased low, so ratios
exaggerate disparity. Set a minimum size
and investigate first.
Write the decision down in a mitigation
decision record. The context with the
measured gap. 3.4 to 4.3 times interval
separate. The decision and the primary
metric. False positive ratio by language
at least 0.8, release blocking. The
alternatives and why they lost. Extra
review for non-English flags was
rejected, too. It delays the group
already burdened. The consequences,
including the cost. Payments accepts
fewer frauds caught with compensating
velocity rules and amount limits. And
the evidence linked, the report, the
tests, and the commit.
Turn the analysis into automated release
gates. False positive and true positive
ratios by language, at least .8. The
same check by region, every intersection
has at least 500 samples or you collect
more data before release. A proxy check
that nothing in the features predicts
language and a performance floor so
fairness never comes from leveling down.
Quick check, why did the region view
show nothing? Pause and think.
Because the gap is driven by language
and language is spread evenly across
regions. Averaging by region hid it.
One more, model A catches more fraud.
Why is it still the worst model? Pause.
Because the gain comes from burdening
innocent non-English customers three to
four times as often while English fraud
slips through.
Let's replay the four pictures. A biased
feature flagged innocent Hinglish
customers over four times as often and
the intervals proved it. The region view
would have hidden it. Removing the proxy
fixed it at a cost decided in the open
and the decision record says why with
evidence.
Next week is explainability and human
oversight starting with how to explain a
model's decisions. Until then, run the
lab and implement the proxy test. Can a
classifier predict language from model
A's features? From model B's? See you in
the next lesson.
